 
Brussel SproutKimchiFermentation
If you think you know Brussels sprouts,prepare to meet them in a completely newway. Most of us grew up with a big“ewwwww!” when it came to brusselsprouts.  Usually they were boiled to deathand could only be resuscitated withslatherings of butter and blizzards of salt. This fermented Brussel Sprout Kimchi recipetakes everything people love about classickimchi—its tang, heat and Gzz, —and pairs itwith one of the most unexpectedly perfectvegetables for fermentation. Brussels sproutkimchi holds its crunch beautifully, soaks upIavor like sponges, and develops an almostnutty sweetness as it ferments.
If you love bold, probiotic-rich Iavors—oryou just want a low-eLort way to level upyour meals—this Brussels Sprout Kimchi isabout to become your new favoritecondiment.With fermenting, especially in the kimchistyle, brussel sprouts can again be adelectable taste treat, and a very healthyone to boot (and don’t worry, this one won’tmake you “boot”). 
I Grst made this as a playful twist ontraditional cabbage kimchi, but it quicklybecame something I love. It’s quick to prep,ferments reliably, and is one of those foodsthat makes people say, “Oooh yah, dat’sgood!” In fact, I gave a dear neighbor of minea taste of this Brussel Sprout Kimchi fermentstraight from the crock and before she leftshe asked four times: “Just one more, OK?” I’ve been making this Brussel Sprout Kimchirecipe for a long time now and Gnd it to bequite forgiving. As long as your vegetablesstay submerged and your fermentationcrock, jar or mason jar stays clean, naturedoes the rest.As members of the brassica family, Brusselssprouts are naturally rich in powerfulcompounds like sulforaphane—renownedfor its potential anticancer properties—andindole-3-carbinol, which supports DNArepair and may help inhibit the growth ofharmful cells. With this kimchi, you get allthe nutritional advantages of raw Brusselssprouts plus the probiotic beneGts offermentation. A double win for Iavor andwellness.
During the fermenting process, these littlegreen gems can soften just enough tobecome pleasantly tender while stillretaining a satisfying bite. Their bold, tangyIavor makes them an unexpected yetirresistible treat.
Serving SuggestionsAdd some to rice bowls, make quirky koreantacos with them, or eat it straight from thejar when no one’s looking (my usual). Servethem as a vibrant hors d’oeuvre, a refreshingside dish, or simply enjoy them straight fromthe jar.For a festive touch, try piling them high inthe center of a platter of roasted beets—thecolors and Iavors can make a stunningholiday presentation.
This recipe is a real gourmet treat!Enjoy!  Pin It!

Add small amt napa cabbageReply ˣfermenTed on October 6, 2013 at 7:59 am said:Hey Tom. Good questions. I would deGnitelytop oL the green beans. Oxygen is generallyyour enemy in fermenting, so keeping yourbeans under the brine in this case would be avery good idea. Not sure of your technique,but for things like this, I often use a masonjar and Gll it completely to the top with brineand then loosely screw on the top so thatgasses and excess liquid can escape.As to storing ferments, I honestly can’tanswer that as I’ve been refrigerating mineonce done, but I’ll share my thoughts. Thepoint is that fermentation will continue inearnest unless you cool it down signiGcantlyat some point, in which case it will simplyslow down. I can’t speak for ALL ferments,but most can go a long time before needingrefrigeration. As sugar/starch suppliesdwindle in the fermenting item, or as thechemistry gradually changes in the fermentitself, you’ll naturally get a die oL of somebacteria, which is Gne, but it will cause somediscoloration. Most ferments will simply getmore and more sour, but I believe the moresour they get, the less they will needrefrigeration for preservation as well. Rootcellars were built in the days beforerefrigeration for a good reason as cooltemperatures help to preserve foods, andprohibit active fermentation. Brussel Sprout Kimchiyield: 2 QUARTS prep time: 30 MINUTESadditional time: 3 SECONDStotal time: 30 MINUTES 3 SECONDSRecipe for making Brussel Sprout kimchi.5.0 Stars (1 Review)
Ingredients2 1/2 lbs brussel sprouts1 medium daikon radish1 1/2 tablespoons diced ginger1 tablespoon diced garlic4 tablespoons Korean red pepperpowder1 tablespoon Gsh sauce or shrimp sauce(I excluded this)Brine2 tablespoons sea salt4 cups water
InstructionsA. Rinse and gently clean the brusselsprouts, daikon, and gingerB. Slice the brussel sprouts in halflengthwiseC. Cut the daikon into disks approx ⒛"thick. If your diakon is particularlyfat then cut lengthwise in half orquarters GrstD. Dissolve the sea salt in the water tomake a brineE. Place the brussel sprouts anddiakon in the brine and leave for afew hours or overnight if you prefer.Do your best to compress theveggies to keep them under thebrine if possible.F. Drain the brine and reserve it forlaterG. Finely dice the ginger and garlicH. In a large bowl, combine the garlicand ginger with the drained veggiesand korean chili powder and toss(this is where you would also addGsh sauce or shrimp sauce if youwish)I. Place everything in a fermentationcrock, 2 one quart mason jars or awide mouth glass jar. Put somepressure on the ingredients withyour Gst or a pickle packer (I lovethese by the way!). Unlike shreddedcabbage ferments, there will likelynot be enough natural liquidreleased to fully cover the brusselsprouts.J. Place a weight on top of the veggiesto keep them compacted them andencourage the brine level to riseabove them. In this image I used alarge clear glass jar for thefermentation so you can see insidethe fermentation vessel.
K. Add back as much of the reservedbrine as necessary until the brusselsprouts are fully covered whilecompacted. In the method picturedI simply used a plastic bag Glled withbrine to act as a weight. If using thismethod, leave the air out of the bagso it can conform to the shape ofyour container. You can of courseuse a fermentation crock with aweight or a mason jars usingweights and an airlock cap.L. Cover with lid or airlock capM. Let this sit and ferment for 2-4weeks. You can let it go longer if youwish. Just taste every once in awhileto see how the Iavor and texturechanges.N. When the taste is as you like it, jar itup and refrigerate to signiGcantlyslow the fermentation process.O. Enjoy!!!!

Maybe I would need to add aculture, possibly from my saurkraut?I have had fermented mung beans whiletraveling abroad, but I am unsure as towhether the Lacto Bacillus on home sproutedbrassicas will be supcient.Thanks for any insight or comments!~SReply ˣfermenTed on January 6, 2017 at 9:08 pm said:That’s a great question Seth, andunfortunately it’s one I don’t have ananswer for. At Grst I was confused sinceyour question is placed on the brusselsprouts comment board. It took me acouple of re-readings to recognize thatyou were talking about fermentingsprouted seeds. I personally haven’t runacross fermented seed sprouts nor have Itried it myself. I honestly don’t see whythey wouldn’t work or be delicious. I thinkyou might be right about needing to add aculture, since sprouts are home madefrom seeds, they perhaps haven’t had timeor opportunity to cultivate a bacterialcontent (no soil contact) so the fermentmay not spring to life in earnest. What I’ddo if I were to try it, would be to simplethrow in a couple of red radishes, or acabbage leaf or two, just to inncoulate theferment. I tend to not add juice fromprevious sauerkrauts since the bacteriathat thrive in fully fermented sauerkrautaren’t ones that would necesarily thrive inthe less acidic early stage ferment like asprout ferment.good luck if you try and please write backif you do. Thanks!Reply ˣeden on January 10, 2017 at 5:13 pm said:hi TedI am very happy I have found your site(already shared it with few of my friends)…Ihave a question: what is the purpose ofsoaking the brussel sprouts; is it necessary?I have added also a bit of dill just to add atwist…my mom told me to freeze them a bitso they lose the bitternessthanksReply ˣfermenTed on January 15, 2017 at 11:20 amsaid:Soaking the brussel sprouts in a brine is atraditional method for making kimchi.Since brussel sprouts won’t compact quiteas well under pressure, it’s a little trickierto get the water level to rise above thebrussel sprouts if you simply salt themand compress them. Soaking them inbrine gets them a little wetter and alsoallows the salt to still start to break downthe cell walls to release more liquid.Mixing the brine also gives you extra liquidto add back in if necessary to cover.Thanks and good luck!Reply ˣMaureen on February 12, 2017 at 2:55 pm said:Dumb question- when Gnished fermentingand transferring to smaller containers, doesit still need to be in lots of liquid? Can it bewithout any liquid?Reply ˣfermenTed on February 13, 2017 at 9:20 pmsaid:Never a dumb question. Thanks for asking.It’s best to keep your ferments in theliquid from the original fermentation.They’ll keep pretty well without beingcovered, largely because they’ve becomemore acidic (lower pH), which keeps themrelatively immune to problems. Mold andyeasts can grow wherever food andoxygen meet, so to ensure safer longerterm storage, keep your fermentssubmerged or close to it.Reply ˣMaureen on February 25, 2017 at 7:16 amsaid:It turned out every bit as delicious asyou said it would!Reply ˣfermenTed on March 2, 2017 at 6:33 amsaid:Excellent!Reply ˣAndi Flanagan on April 10, 2020 at 11:37 am said:My Brussels Sprout Kimchi has been in thefridge after fermenting for 4 weeks, for TWOyears and they are still too hard to eat!
